name: Francoist Spain
info: The Spanish State ruled by Francisco Franco, first in the Nationalist-held territories during the Spanish Civil War and then over all Spain until his death in 1975, a single-party dictatorship of National Catholicism and repression.

facts.founder: Francisco Franco, recognised as Caudillo of Spain by the Junta de Defensa Nacional on 1 October 1936
facts.predecessor: Second Spanish Republic; in the Nationalist zone, the Junta de Defensa Nacional
facts.successor: Kingdom of Spain under Juan Carlos, through the Spanish transition to democracy

t: The regime grew out of the Nationalist side of the Spanish Civil War: Franco was recognised as Caudillo on 1 October 1936 and in April 1937 merged the Falange and the Carlists into the FET y de las JONS, the sole legal party.

Victory in 1939 was followed by mass imprisonment, executions and exile; by the regime's own figures more than 270,000 people were held in prisons and some 500,000 had fled, and more than 200,000 Spaniards are estimated to have died from 1940 to 1942 of persecution, hunger and disease.

After isolation and autarky, the liberalisation of 1959 opened the "Spanish Miracle" of the 1960s, but political parties and independent unions stayed banned until Franco's death on 20 November 1975 opened the transition to democracy.
dyk: Under the Law of Political Responsibility of February 1939, parishes were granted policing powers equal to those of local officials and Falange leaders, and some official jobs required a statement of "good behaviour" from a priest.
ev: The Junta de Defensa Nacional, governing the Nationalist-held territories, recognises Franco as Caudillo of Spain on 1 October
In April Franco merges the Falange Española de las JONS with the Carlist Comunión Tradicionalista to form the Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS
The Nationalists win the Spanish Civil War, and the Falange is declared the sole legally sanctioned party
Franco and Hitler meet at Hendaye on 23 October, but the talks on Spain's entry into the Second World War end in failure
Spain is declared a kingdom on 26 July, with Franco as regent for life and the sole right to appoint his successor
Under pressure from the United States, the IMF and the technocrats of Opus Dei, the regime liberalises the economy
Franco designates Juan Carlos of Bourbon as his heir, and Spain closes its border with Gibraltar
Franco dies on 20 November, and Juan Carlos becomes King of Spain

sections.foundation:
The regime emerged from the Nationalist side in the Spanish Civil War. On 1 October 1936 the Junta de Defensa Nacional, which governed the territories the Nationalists held, recognised Francisco Franco as Caudillo of Spain, the Spanish equivalent of the Duce and the Führer. In April 1937 Franco took control of the Falange Española de las JONS, whose founder José Antonio Primo de Rivera had been executed by the Republican government in November 1936, and merged it with the Carlist Comunión Tradicionalista into the Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS, the main component of the Movimiento Nacional. The new government was a one-party dictatorship explicitly modelled on Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, with its own Spanish characteristics.

The Nationalists took the whole of Spain through a methodical war of attrition that involved imprisoning and executing Spaniards found guilty of supporting the values of the Republic: regional autonomy, democracy, free elections and women's rights. The right called these "enemy elements" an "anti-Spain" born of Bolsheviks and a "Judeo-Masonic conspiracy". When the war ended in 1939, by the regime's own figures more than 270,000 people were held in prisons and some 500,000 had fled into exile; between six and seven thousand exiles died in Mauthausen.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Civil War had ravaged the economy, and for more than a decade after it the economy improved little. Franco pursued a fascist-style autarky on the Italian and German models that cut off almost all international trade and aid, and a famine killed over 200,000 people while only black marketeers prospered. In 1940 the Sindicato Vertical became the only legal trade union, under government control. The Instituto Nacional de Colonización, created in 1939, irrigated land and installed settlers in around 300 settlements between 1940 and 1970, while protecting large landowners from expropriation.

On the brink of bankruptcy, pressure from the United States, which gave about $1.5 billion in aid between 1954 and 1964, from the IMF and from technocrats of Opus Dei led the regime to liberalise the economy in 1959, over Franco's opposition. Growth took off in the "Spanish Miracle": international firms opened factories, and in the 1960s Spain was the second-fastest-growing economy in the world after Japan, alongside Brazil. Mass emigration to other European countries relieved surplus population and sent home remittances. Regions such as Madrid, Catalonia and the Basque Country fared far better than Extremadura, Galicia or Andalusia. Divorce, contraception and abortion were forbidden.
sections.military:
Franco cut the army from almost one million at the end of the Civil War to 250,000 in early 1940, most of them two-year conscripts. In November 1942, with the Allied landings in North Africa and the German occupation of France, he ordered a partial mobilisation that brought the army to over 750,000 men; the Air Force and Navy grew to 35,000 airmen and 25,000 sailors by 1945, and the army kept about 400,000 men until the end of the Second World War.

Spain remained formally non-belligerent or neutral in that war but in practice supported the Axis. Franco seriously considered joining for the sake of ideology and of claims to Gibraltar, French Morocco and the Oran district of Algeria, and took over the international city of Tangier after the defeat of France. The Meeting at Hendaye with Hitler on 23 October 1940 ended in failure over Franco's demands and Germany's own, and a further attempt in December 1940 for Operation Felix also failed. Spain still sent the Blue Division to fight on the Eastern Front, let German submarines use its ports and sent tungsten and foodstuffs to Germany. In Africa it gave up its protectorate in Morocco in 1956 and granted Equatorial Guinea independence in 1968.
sections.governance:
Franco ruled with, on paper, more power than any Spanish leader before or since; Stanley G. Payne judged that the absence of even a rubber-stamp parliament in the early years made his government "the most purely arbitrary in the world". The Constituent Law of the Cortes of 1942 created a purely advisory Cortes Españolas, elected by neither direct nor universal suffrage, and ministers were appointed and dismissed by Franco alone. The referendum law of 1945, in which only heads of families could vote, was used in 1947 to revive the monarchy with Franco as regent for life, and in 1966 to approve a new organic law creating the modern office of Prime Minister. Spain was one of the most centralised countries in Europe: Franco abolished regional autonomy and the fueros of Guipuzcoa and Biscay, classed as "traitor regions".

Catholicism was the state religion, and the Church controlled the schools; the Ministry of Education under José Ibáñez Martín purged thousands of teachers. Women lost the rights the Republic had given them and could not become judges, and from 1941 the Women's Protection Board confined tens of thousands of girls and young women in centres where they were routinely brutalised. Homosexuality was criminalised from the Penal Code of 1944, and the Press Law of 1938 imposed prior censorship.
sections.impact:
Franco's nationalism promoted a Castilian-centric unitary national identity by repressing Spain's diversity. The government revoked the official status the Republic had given Basque, Galician and Catalan, forbade other languages in schools, documents, religious ceremonies and signs, and promoted bullfighting and flamenco as national traditions. For nearly twenty years the regime presented the Civil War as a crusade against Bolshevism in defence of Christian civilisation, the central myth of a national rebirth. The silence imposed on families of the Republic was carried into the 1977 Pact of Forgetting.

Historians long debated its nature. Until 1964 it was commonly defined as totalitarian and fascist; Juan José Linz then called it authoritarian, with "limited political pluralism", and Payne called its first phase "semi-fascist". Paul Preston and Julián Casanova later placed it in the family of European fascism, and Martin Blinkhorn calls it "the only European regime with a major radical fascist ingredient to survive long beyond 1945". The regime supported neo-fascist movements in Europe up to the 1960s and the "ratlines" for war criminals. The Argentine General Juan Carlos Onganía modelled his military regime of 1966–1970 on Francoist Spain, and Francoism influenced Chile's military dictatorship.
sections.decline:
Ties to the Axis brought isolation after 1945: Spain was explicitly condemned in a United Nations resolution of 1946 and was not admitted until 1955. The Cold War changed this, as Franco's anti-communism tilted the regime towards the United States in the early 1950s. On 26 July 1947 Spain was declared a kingdom with the throne left vacant; Franco passed over Infante Juan, Count of Barcelona, whom he found too liberal, and in 1969 named Juan Carlos of Bourbon his heir. The Press and Print Law of 1966 ended prior censorship but kept controls, and the restrictions on languages and on women eased somewhat in the 1960s and 1970s.

In 1973 Franco resigned as Prime Minister and named Admiral Luis Carrero Blanco, who was meant to continue the regime, but ETA assassinated him the same year and Carlos Arias Navarro took his place. In 1975 Morocco took control of the former Spanish territories in the Sahara after the Green March. Franco died on 20 November 1975, and Juan Carlos, now King, began the transition that made Spain a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament and devolved governments. The Historical Memory Law of 2007 sought official recognition of the regime's crimes against civilians and a state-supervised search for mass graves.

summary: Francoist Spain was the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, born in the Nationalist zone in 1936 and ruling all Spain from 1939 to 1975. Built on a single party, the Church and the army, it imprisoned and executed its opponents, repressed regional languages and women's rights, kept to the Axis side of neutrality in the Second World War, and after 1959 presided over rapid economic growth.
references: Stanley G. Payne, The Franco Regime, 1936–1975 (University of Wisconsin Press, 1987)
Paul Preston, Franco: A Biography (Basic Books, 1994)
Enrique Moradiellos, La España de Franco (1939–1975). Política y Sociedad (Síntesis, 2000)
Javier Tusell, Historia de España en el Siglo XX. 3: La Dictadura de Franco (Santillana, 1999)
Michael Richards, The Splintering of Spain: Cultural History and the Spanish Civil War, 1936–1939 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)

pointDescs.1936: Franco is recognised as Caudillo by the Junta de Defensa Nacional, which governs the territories the Nationalists hold.
pointDescs.1937: The Falange and the Carlists are merged into the FET y de las JONS, the regime's single party.
pointDescs.1939: The Nationalists win the Civil War and rule the whole of Spain; more than 270,000 people are held in prisons.
pointDescs.1940: The army is cut to 250,000, autarky and famine cripple the economy, and the meeting at Hendaye fails to bring Spain into the war.
pointDescs.1942: Franco orders a partial mobilisation that brings the army to over 750,000 men, and the Cortes Españolas are established.
pointDescs.1946: The United Nations condemns the regime and denies it recognition, leaving Spain isolated.
pointDescs.1947: Spain is declared a kingdom, and a referendum makes Franco regent for life.
pointDescs.1954: American aid begins, about $1.5 billion by 1964, as the Cold War brings Spain into alliance with the United States.
pointDescs.1955: Spain is admitted to the United Nations.
pointDescs.1959: The economy is liberalised, opening the way to massive foreign investment and rapid growth.
pointDescs.1966: A referendum approves a new organic law, and the Press and Print Law ends prior censorship, as the Spanish Miracle gathers pace.
pointDescs.1969: Franco names Juan Carlos of Bourbon his heir and closes the border with Gibraltar, at the height of the 1960s growth.
pointDescs.1973: Franco hands the premiership to Luis Carrero Blanco, who is assassinated by ETA the same year.
pointDescs.1975: Morocco takes the Spanish Sahara after the Green March, and Franco's death on 20 November opens the transition to democracy.

notes: The article names no capital; Madrid is given as the seat of the ministers and government after 1939. No wartime seat is given, so none is named.
The saved article's Sources and Further reading sections are empty, so references are [].

The colonial paragraph is garbled (Mohammed V 'invaded Spanish Sahara during the Ifni War' 'the year after' 1969; 'Sid Infi'); only the dated Moroccan protectorate (1956), Equatorial Guinea (1968) and Green March (1975) are used.
The fascism debate is kept as the article's attributed views (Linz, Payne, Preston, Casanova, Blinkhorn), not as a verdict.
The famine figure (over 200,000) and the 1940-1942 death estimate (more than 200,000) may overlap; each is given in its own context.
